changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For ticketing and event buyers (especially COO/operations): "A name, not a queue. Your person, their backup, and someone watching at minute four of every major on-sale." Lead with named people and the escalation path, not tiers or response times. Confirm with Support leadership that named, event-based on-call coverage exists or can be packaged before using.
changes.why: Halima asked "who's my person," was shown tiered support plans, and dismissed them as "a queue with a faster timer." Her own words were "a name, not a queue" and "someone who picks up."

changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: For ticketing and event operations buyers, open with the incident instead of global growth: "Payments fail four minutes into your on-sale. Who answers?"
changes.why: The deal started when payments failed minutes into an on-sale, no human answered, and the CEO saw it on social. That made it a who-answers problem owned by the COO, not a global-growth decision.

changes.change: For COO/operations buyers in ticketing and events, add an "On-sale morning" plan as a proof point: who's watching, who you call, and what happens at minute four. Pair it with the line "You don't buy uptime, you buy what happens when it's down." We need to build the plan with a solutions engineer before this copy can be used.
changes.why: Halima rejected uptime framing ("I buy what happens when it's down") and wanted a minute-four plan. We had no such plan, though the rep could have built one with our solutions engineer.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For ticketing and event buyers, stop leading with logos and customer stories. Lead instead with a referenceable ticketing customer who will describe who picked up during their peak event. Until we have one, lead with the named people from the M5 replacement.
changes.why: The rep had logos but not a person. The competitor won the conversation by putting named people in the room, which moved the customer's questions from throughput to names.
